"MASTER GAME DEVELOPMENT PROMPT

PART 1 OF 4 — CORE GAME DESIGN, LANDSCAPE CONFIGURATION, CONTROLS, MOVEMENT AND COMBAT

You are developing a complete 2D side-scrolling action roguelike game inspired by the Naruto universe.

The gameplay should take strong mechanical inspiration from Dead Cells: responsive movement, challenging combat, interconnected rooms, branching routes, precise dodging, parrying, combos, aerial combat, powerful enemies, boss encounters, and a progression system built around collecting abilities and improving builds.

This must feel like a real action roguelike, not a generic RPG, not a turn-based game, not an arena fighter, and not a basic platformer with a few abilities.

The game must be designed specifically for mobile devices.

---

1. ABSOLUTE SCREEN ORIENTATION REQUIREMENTS

THIS SECTION HAS THE HIGHEST PRIORITY. DO NOT IGNORE IT.

The entire game must use a horizontal LANDSCAPE orientation.

- Lock the project orientation to landscape.
- Never generate portrait gameplay.
- Never generate portrait menus.
- Never rotate the camera into portrait mode.
- Never place the main gameplay interface vertically.
- Never use a default portrait mobile-game template.
- Every gameplay screen, menu, inventory, customization screen, reward screen, and pause menu must be designed horizontally.

If the development environment has a default portrait configuration, override it before creating the game.

1.1 Screen proportions

Use these reference resolutions:

- Target display resolution: 1920 × 1080.
- Internal pixel-art rendering resolution: 480 × 270.
- Logical UI coordinate system: 960 × 540.
- Aspect ratio: 16:9.

The game must also support wider mobile displays, including 18:9, 19.5:9, and 20:9.

For wider screens:

- Expand the visible environment horizontally.
- Keep the central gameplay composition consistent.
- Do not stretch characters, sprites, backgrounds, or UI.
- Do not distort the aspect ratio.
- Keep buttons inside safe screen boundaries.

1.2 Camera

Use a 2D side-view camera.

The player should normally remain around 35–45% of the screen width, leaving enough visible space ahead to anticipate enemies and obstacles.

Camera behavior:

- Smooth horizontal follow.
- Slight vertical adjustment when jumping or falling.
- Do not make the camera rotate.
- Do not use a top-down camera.
- Do not use an isometric camera.
- Keep bosses and important enemies visible whenever possible.
- Avoid excessive camera shake.
- Use controlled camera movement during boss attacks and major events.

The environment must scroll horizontally as the player moves through the level.

1.3 Screen layout

All interface elements must be arranged for horizontal gameplay.

Top-left:

- Health bar.
- Chakra bar.
- Stamina bar.
- Player level.
- Small status effects.

Top-center:

- Current chapter.
- Current room name.
- Current objective.

Top-right:

- Currency.
- Map button.
- Pause button.
- Optional progression indicators.

Bottom-left:

- Virtual movement joystick.

Bottom-right:

- Combat buttons.
- Skill buttons.
- Jump.
- Dash.
- Block/Parry.

The center of the screen must remain as clear as possible so the player can see the character, enemies, attacks, and environment.

1.4 Character proportions

Characters must be designed as side-view pixel-art sprites.

Suggested sprite dimensions:

Character type| Approximate sprite size
Player| 32 × 48 px
Small enemy| 32 × 40 px
Standard enemy| 40 × 48 px
Elite enemy| 48 × 64 px
Mini-boss| 80–112 px
Standard boss| 128–192 px
Bijuu| 256 × 192 px or larger

These are reference sizes, not mandatory limits.

Characters must be readable at the internal rendering resolution.

1.5 Required orientation validation

Before implementing the rest of the game, verify:

1. The project is locked to landscape.
2. The camera is side-view.
3. The joystick is positioned on the left.
4. Combat buttons are positioned on the right.
5. The environment scrolls horizontally.
6. All menus are landscape.
7. The HUD is horizontal.
8. No default portrait UI elements remain.

Do not proceed with a portrait-based prototype.

---

2. GAMEPLAY IDENTITY

The main gameplay loop must be:

1. Enter a mission.
2. Explore interconnected rooms.
3. Fight enemies.
4. Collect rewards.
5. Choose branching paths.
6. Improve the current run.
7. Encounter stronger enemies.
8. Defeat bosses.
9. Unlock permanent progression.
10. Continue toward the final objective or die and restart.

The game should reward skill, timing, positioning, and strategic ability combinations.

Combat must be fast, responsive, and challenging.

Enemies must be able to punish careless attacks.

The player must be able to:

- Move left and right.
- Jump.
- Double jump when unlocked.
- Dash.
- Block.
- Parry.
- Perform light attacks.
- Perform heavy attacks.
- Perform aerial attacks.
- Use ninja tools.
- Use chakra abilities.
- Switch between equipped skills.
- Chain attacks into combos.
- Cancel certain animations into defensive actions.

Every action must have a clear animation and gameplay purpose.

---

3. MOBILE CONTROL SYSTEM

The controls must be designed specifically for touchscreen devices.

The interface must remain on the lower portions of the landscape screen without covering important gameplay information.

All buttons must have:

- Clear visual states.
- Press animations.
- Responsive input.
- Configurable opacity.
- Adjustable size.
- Adjustable position.
- Optional vibration feedback.
- Consistent spacing.

Players must be able to customize the control layout.

3.1 Virtual joystick

Position: bottom-left.

Reference configuration:

- Diameter: 104 logical UI units.
- Left margin: 80 units.
- Bottom margin: 90 units.

The joystick must support:

- Left movement.
- Right movement.
- Neutral position.
- Optional directional input for aerial movement.

Use a floating or fixed joystick, depending on which implementation is more reliable.

3.2 Main attack button

Position: bottom-right.

Reference configuration:

- Diameter: 68 units.
- Right margin: 85 units.
- Bottom margin: 90 units.

Function: Light Attack.

Repeated presses must create a combo.

3.3 Heavy attack button

Position: immediately left of the main attack button.

Reference diameter: 64 units.

Function: Heavy Attack.

Heavy attacks must be slower and more powerful than light attacks.

3.4 Jump button

Position: above the main attack button.

Reference diameter: 66 units.

Function: Jump.

Allow the player to jump while moving.

3.5 Dash button

Position: below the jump button.

Reference diameter: 62 units.

Function: Dash.

The dash must follow the player's directional input.

3.6 Block and Parry button

Position: above the heavy attack button.

Reference diameter: 68 units.

This is one defensive button with two different functions:

- Holding the button activates Block.
- Pressing it with precise timing activates Parry.

Do not create separate block and parry buttons.

3.7 Skill buttons

Provide two primary skill buttons.

- Skill 1: approximately 60 units.
- Skill 2: approximately 60 units.

They must be positioned around the right-side combat controls without overlapping the main attack button.

3.8 Chakra button

Reference diameter: 56 units.

Use this button for a configured chakra-related action, such as chakra charging or a special ability activation, depending on the selected build.

3.9 Button customization

Allow players to:

- Increase button size up to 140%.
- Decrease button size down to 70%.
- Move buttons within safe screen boundaries.
- Change button opacity.
- Restore default positions.

Save control settings permanently.

---

4. MOVEMENT SYSTEM

Movement must feel similar in responsiveness to a polished action platformer.

Use these initial reference values:

Property| Base value
Horizontal movement speed| 220 px/s
Acceleration| 1800 px/s²
Air control| 85%
Gravity| 1200 px/s²
Jump force| 480
Maximum falling speed| 650

These values should be adjustable during balancing.

4.1 Ground movement

- Smooth acceleration.
- Responsive stopping.
- No excessive sliding.
- No delayed directional input.
- Character animation must match movement speed.

4.2 Jumping

The player must have a responsive jump.

Requirements:

- Variable jump height if the jump button is held.
- Short input buffering.
- Coyote time of approximately 0.10 seconds.
- Proper landing animations.
- Different aerial attack animations.

4.3 Advanced movement

Additional movement abilities may be unlocked through progression:

- Double Jump.
- Wall Jump.
- Wall Slide.
- Air Dash.
- Chakra-enhanced movement.
- Temporary movement buffs.

These abilities must not all be available automatically at the beginning.

4.4 Environmental interaction

The player must be able to:

- Stand on platforms.
- Fall through designated platforms.
- Jump between different heights.
- Climb designated passages.
- Enter doors and room transitions.
- Interact with objects.
- Activate checkpoints.
- Discover hidden passages.

Every platform and passage must be physically reachable.

Do not generate impossible jumps or inaccessible rewards.

---

5. DASH SYSTEM

Dash is a core defensive and mobility mechanic.

Initial configuration:

Property| Value
Duration| 0.30 seconds
Distance| Approximately 105 px
Cooldown| 0.70 seconds
Invulnerability duration| 0.16 seconds

Requirements:

- Dash horizontally by default.
- Allow diagonal dash when directional input is provided.
- Support ground dash.
- Support air dash when unlocked or configured.
- Create a brief visual afterimage.
- Prevent the player from being permanently invulnerable.
- Use a clear cooldown indicator.

The dash may cancel certain attack recovery animations, but it must not cancel every action without restrictions.

Some boss attacks must require correct timing rather than simply allowing the player to dash continuously.

---

6. BLOCK AND PARRY SYSTEM

Block and Parry are essential mechanics.

They must be implemented as two outcomes of the same defensive button.

6.1 Block

Holding the defensive button activates Block.

Initial values:

- Reduce incoming damage by 70%.
- Maximum stamina: 100.
- Blocking consumes 12 stamina per second.
- Stamina regeneration: 25 per second when not blocking.

Additional rules:

- Blocking reduces knockback.
- Blocking does not eliminate all damage.
- Certain powerful attacks break through guard.
- Some attacks cause additional stamina loss.
- The player cannot block indefinitely.

If stamina reaches zero, the player enters a short guard-break state.

6.2 Parry

A Parry happens when the defensive button is pressed at the correct moment.

Initial perfect-parry window:

- 0.12 seconds.

A successful Parry must:

1. Negate an eligible incoming attack.
2. Play a unique defensive animation.
3. Produce a clear visual effect.
4. Play a distinct sound effect.
5. Briefly stun the attacker.
6. Restore 15 stamina.
7. Restore 5 chakra.

Parry timing must be skill-based.

Do not allow players to hold the button and automatically parry everything.

6.3 Failed Parry

If the player presses the defensive button too early or too late:

- It may become a normal Block if the button remains held.
- Normal stamina requirements still apply.
- The player must not receive the benefits of a successful Parry.

6.4 Attack compatibility

Not every attack must be parryable.

Use these rules:

- Light attacks can generally be blocked.
- Some light attacks may be parried, depending on the enemy.
- Heavy attacks can be parried with precise timing when explicitly designed to allow it.
- Certain large attacks must be avoided with movement or Dash.
- Environmental attacks cannot automatically be parried.
- Ultimate attacks must have clear visual telegraphs.

Enemies must communicate their attack type through animation and visual effects.

A parryable attack should have a recognizable timing cue.

---

7. COMBAT SYSTEM

Combat must be based on responsive action-game mechanics.

Every attack must have:

- Startup frames.
- Active frames.
- Recovery frames.
- Hitbox.
- Damage.
- Knockback.
- Hitstun.
- Animation.
- Sound effect.
- Visual effect.

Avoid attacks that simply subtract health without meaningful interaction.

7.1 Light attack combo

The basic combo contains four attacks.

Hit| Damage
First hit| 10
Second hit| 12
Third hit| 14
Fourth hit| 18

Initial timing:

- Attack duration: approximately 0.35 seconds.
- Recovery: approximately 0.18 seconds.

The final hit should have stronger knockback.

The player must be able to chain attacks by pressing the attack button at the appropriate time.

If the player waits too long, the combo resets.

7.2 Heavy attack

Initial configuration:

- Damage: 25.
- Duration: approximately 0.70 seconds.
- Recovery: approximately 0.35 seconds.

Heavy attacks must:

- Deal higher damage.
- Have slower startup.
- Have stronger knockback.
- Be useful against armored enemies.
- Create a more noticeable impact effect.

Heavy attacks must not become universally superior to light attacks.

7.3 Aerial attacks

The player can attack while airborne.

Initial aerial attack damage: 12.

Aerial attacks should support:

- Short aerial combos.
- Enemy knockback.
- Air-to-ground transitions.
- Different animations from ground attacks.

7.4 Dash attack

Initial damage: 15.

The Dash Attack should be a special follow-up action, not a replacement for normal movement.

7.5 Hit reactions

Characters must react to attacks.

Include:

- Light hitstun.
- Heavy hitstun.
- Knockback.
- Launching.
- Grounded recovery.
- Guard break.
- Boss stagger.

Bosses must have specific resistance rules so that players cannot permanently stun-lock them.

7.6 Attack cancellation

Allow limited animation cancellation.

Examples:

- Light attack into Dash.
- Certain attacks into Jump.
- Certain attacks into Block.
- Skill attacks into movement after recovery.

Do not allow unrestricted cancellation of every animation.

Combat must reward good timing and positioning.

---

8. PLAYER ATTRIBUTES

The player begins with these base attributes:

Attribute| Base value
Health| 100
Chakra| 100
Stamina| 100
Chakra regeneration| 3 per second
Health regeneration| None

Health does not regenerate automatically by default.

Healing must come from specific items, rewards, abilities, or designated healing rooms.

8.1 Damage categories

Support different damage types:

- Physical.
- Fire.
- Wind.
- Lightning.
- Earth.
- Water.
- Yin.
- Yang.
- Poison.
- Explosive.
- Special chakra damage.

Enemies may have resistances and weaknesses.

Damage calculations must be consistent and readable.

8.2 Critical hits

Include a critical-hit system.

Critical chance and critical damage can be improved through temporary run upgrades and permanent progression.

Critical hits must have clear visual feedback.

---

9. DIFFICULTY SYSTEM

Provide these difficulty levels:

Difficulty| Enemy health| Enemy damage
Easy| 75%| 70%
Normal| 100%| 100%
Hard| 140%| 130%
Nightmare| 190%| 170%
Legendary| 250%| 220%

Difficulty must affect more than health and damage.

Higher difficulties must also introduce:

- More aggressive enemy behavior.
- Different enemy combinations.
- More dangerous room hazards.
- More complex boss patterns.
- Reduced healing opportunities where appropriate.
- Better rewards.
- Additional elite encounters.

Do not simply multiply enemy health and call that a difficulty system.

---

10. WEAPON SYSTEM

The player can equip two weapons or weapon slots, depending on the selected equipment configuration.

Supported weapon categories:

- Kunai.
- Shuriken.
- Katana.
- Dual Blades.
- Chakra Blade.
- Heavy Sword.
- Staff.
- Other original ninja tools.

Example base weapon values:

Weapon| Damage| Characteristics
Kunai| 10| Fast, short range
Katana| 20| Balanced
Heavy Sword| 35| Slow, powerful
Shuriken| 8| Ranged projectile

These are starting balance values.

Each weapon must have:

- Unique attack animations.
- Unique attack speed.
- Unique range.
- Unique hitboxes.
- Unique sound effects.
- Different strengths and weaknesses.

Weapons must be visually represented on the character when equipped.

Weapons may be improved through rewards and permanent progression.

Do not make every weapon function identically with only different damage numbers.

---

11. ENEMY AI

Enemies must have functional behavior.

They must not simply stand still and repeatedly attack.

Each enemy type should have:

- Detection range.
- Movement behavior.
- Attack range.
- Attack cooldown.
- Defensive behavior.
- Hit reactions.
- Attack telegraphs.
- Death animation.
- Reward configuration.

Enemy archetypes may include:

1. Basic rogue ninja.
2. Melee shinobi.
3. Ranged kunai user.
4. Sword fighter.
5. Fast assassin.
6. Defensive warrior.
7. Chakra caster.
8. Summoner.
9. Poison specialist.
10. Explosive specialist.
11. Elite shinobi.
12. Mini-boss.

Enemies must be able to:

- Approach the player.
- Maintain appropriate attack distance.
- Attack.
- Retreat when appropriate.
- React to blocking and parrying.
- React to knockback.
- Use special abilities.
- Coordinate with other enemies when necessary.

Different enemies must have different attack patterns.

---

12. PIXEL ART AND ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS

Use polished, consistent pixel art.

Visual direction:

- Detailed pixel-art environments.
- Strong silhouettes.
- Readable characters.
- Fluid combat animations.
- Distinct enemy designs.
- Clear attack effects.
- Layered backgrounds.
- Atmospheric lighting.
- Controlled particle effects.

Use the Naruto universe as the thematic foundation, but create original game assets rather than copying Dead Cells assets.

Required animation states include:

- Idle.
- Run.
- Jump.
- Fall.
- Land.
- Light attacks.
- Heavy attacks.
- Aerial attacks.
- Dash.
- Block.
- Parry.
- Hit reaction.
- Knockback.
- Skill activation.
- Death.

Animation must match gameplay timing.

Do not use one generic animation for every attack.

---

13. TECHNICAL QUALITY REQUIREMENTS

Target platform: Android mobile devices.

Performance target: 60 FPS.

The game must:

- Use optimized 2D rendering.
- Avoid unnecessary particle effects.
- Pool frequently created projectiles and effects where possible.
- Avoid excessive memory allocation during combat.
- Keep controls responsive.
- Maintain stable frame pacing.
- Support different landscape screen ratios.
- Save player progression.
- Avoid losing saved data after closing the game.

Do not sacrifice gameplay responsiveness for unnecessary visual effects.

---

14. DEVELOPMENT RULES

The development AI must follow these rules:

1. Do not create the entire game as one rushed implementation.
2. Build and test one system at a time.
3. Do not create fake buttons or nonfunctional menus.
4. Do not leave important mechanics as placeholders.
5. Do not silently remove requirements.
6. Do not replace complex mechanics with generic approximations.
7. Keep systems modular and compatible with future additions.
8. Preserve existing functionality when adding new systems.
9. Test all controls on an actual mobile-sized landscape layout.
10. Prioritize playable functionality over decorative elements.

The first playable prototype must contain:

- Landscape orientation.
- Side-view camera.
- One playable character.
- Horizontal movement.
- Jumping.
- Basic enemy.
- Light attacks.
- Heavy attacks.
- Dash.
- Block.
- Parry.
- Health.
- Chakra.
- Stamina.
- One functional room.

Only after these systems work correctly should the project expand.

END OF PART 1 OF 4.

Continue with Part 2 of this same master document. Do not rewrite, remove, or contradict Part 1.

---
This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.

Screenshots for your own checks: save small JPEGs (a .jpg path, viewport at most 1280px wide) and read only the latest one; older images are dropped from context. Read a full-size PNG only when fine detail matters.
"

1: ## Process lifecycle
2: 
3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.
6: 
7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable 2D landscape side-scrolling action roguelike prototype inspired by Naruto and Dead Cells.

## Requirements
- Android/mobile-first 16:9 landscape gameplay with 480×270 internal rendering and 960×540 logical UI.
- Side-view camera, lower-screen touch controls, horizontal scrolling, and horizontally arranged menus/HUD.
- Implement movement, jumping, dash, block/parry, light/heavy/air attacks, chakra, stamina, health, enemies, boss, and combat feedback.
- Preserve modular systems and playable functionality over placeholders.

## Decisions
- Implemented as a dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript canvas game.
- Used original pixel-style visuals with a shinobi/village aesthetic.
- Added fixed touch controls plus keyboard support for desktop testing.
- Added title, pause, victory, defeat, HUD, difficulty selection, and basic reward screen states.

## Work State
### Completed
- Created the initial playable canvas game in `index.html`, `style.css`, and `game.js`.
- Implemented landscape enforcement, responsive rendering, title screen, camera follow, HUD, touch controls, and keyboard controls.
- Implemented ground movement, jumping, variable input, coyote time, double-jump support, platforms, and dash.
- Implemented light attack combos, heavy attacks, aerial attacks, hitboxes, critical hits, knockback, particles, floating damage, and attack-hit gating.
- Implemented block stamina, parry timing, guard break, enemy damage reactions, projectiles, pickups, enemy AI, and boss encounter logic.
- Implemented pause controls, button opacity/size settings, reset layout, abandon run, victory/defeat states, and room progression.

### Active
- None.

### Blocked
- Visual and runtime verification has not been completed in a browser.
- The prototype still needs Playwright screenshot inspection and console/runtime validation.

## Next Move
1. Start or verify the web server on port 3002.
2. Open the game with Playwright and capture a landscape screenshot.
3. Inspect the screenshot for layout, rendering, and empty-canvas issues.
4. Test keyboard and touch behavior, including death, victory, pause, and boss encounter paths.
5. Fix any runtime JavaScript or layout defects found during verification.

## Relevant Files
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/index.html`: Game entry document and canvas shell.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/style.css`: Landscape viewport, pixel rendering, portrait blocking, and toast styling.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/game.js`: Complete gameplay, rendering, controls, AI, combat, UI, and game states.

## Important Context
- The user requested the complete Part 1 prototype, not further Part 2+ content.
- The game is unverified and may contain runtime or syntax defects that need browser testing.
- Key internal symbols include `player`, `enemies`, `startRun()`, `update()`, `draw()`, `takeDamage()`, and `hurtEnemy()`.
- The project currently has no framework or build dependencies; it serves as static files.
